title: Permissionless Verifiable Information Dispersal (Data Availability for Bitcoin Rollups)
abstract: Rollups are special applications on distributed state machines (aka blockchains) for which the underlying state machine only logs, but does not execute, transactions. Rollups scale throughput by using auxiliary machines that have higher throughput and lower cost of executing transactions than the underlying blockchain. State updates are periodically posted to the underlying blockchain and either verified directly through succinct cryptographic proofs (zk rollups) or can be challenged for a defined period of time in a verifiable way by third parties (optimistic rollups). However, once computation is reduced, communication quickly becomes the new bottleneck. The critical service that the underlying blockchain provides, in addition to verification, is data availability: that necessary data can always be recovered upon request. However, directly broadcasting data requires communication per participant that is linear in the data size. Verifiable information dispersal (VID) systems achieve sublinear blowup in the Ethereum's security and same participation model, where all nodes have a strong public-key identity. However, it is not known how to do so in the permissionless model (the Bitcoin model), where participants are unauthenticated and participation is dynamic. We construct a VID system that is secure under the same model as Bitcoin, with one minimal additional requirement on the existence of reliable participants. Our system uses a state machine replication (SMR) protocol (e.g., Bitcoin) as a black box, and is therefore backward compatible. We implemented the system on top of Bitcoin core with the Regression Test Network (regtest), and our analysis shows that it can reduce communication costs and latency up to more than 1, 000× and 10×, respectively, for certain parameter choices. 1983 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

However, directly broadcasting data requires communication per participant that is linear in the data size. Verifiable information dispersal (VID) systems achieve sublin- ear blowup in the Ethereum's security and same participation model, where all nodes have a strong public-key identity. Introduction Rollups are special applications on distributed state ma- chines (aka blockchains) for which the underlying state machine only logs, but does not execute transactions [29], [37]. They are said to operate on the Layer 2 (L2) on top of the underlying Layer 1 (L1) blockchain. L1s (e.g., Bitcoin [31], Ethereum [39]) are general-purpose decentralized VMs but have high transaction costs and limited throughput due to redundant execution by all nodes. Recently, rollups have become a popular way to scale applications on Ethereum [39] and there is now growing interest in running rollups on Bitcoin [31]. Rollups introduce one or more auxiliary servers that execute transactions and periodically post underlying state updates to the L1 along with compressed transaction data. There are two flavors for handling these updates. Validity rollups (aka zk rollups [38], [15]) create succinct cryp- tographic proofs , proving that the update is correct. In optimistic rollups [26] the L1 accepts updates optimistically, but accepts challenges from third parties about updates being incorrect. Rollups scale throughput and reduce transaction costs by using auxiliary machines with higher throughput and lower cost of executing transactions than the underlying blockchain [11]. Blockchains like Ethereum or Bitcoin have extremely low throughput and high cost because (a) the hardware requirements for operating a node are deliberately capped to encourage large and diverse participation (decen- tralization) and (b) the price a user pays for a transaction must cover the operational cost of all participating nodes executing that transaction, which is redundant. 1 Thus, a rollup can achieve higher throughput and lower- cost transactions than its underlying L1 while still inheriting security from the L1. There are several considerations in deploying a rollup on one L1 versus another (e.g., Bit- coin vs Ethereum). First, different L1s achieve different security properties (e.g., Bitcoin is more permissionless than Ethereum). Second, L1 assets can be transferred on rollups without introducing new security assumptions (e.g., malicious rollup operators cannot steal or double-spend these assets). For example, a user can deposit ETH into a rollup on Ethereum by locking it in a smart contract whose internal accounting is controlled by the rollup. This user can transfer this ETH to other rollup users more cheaply than on Ethereum directly. At any time a user that now holds the ETH can withdraw it from the smart contract. This does not rely on any new trust assumptions beyond Ethereum. Similarly, a rollup on Bitcoin could allow users to cheaply transfer BTC without new trust assumptions beyond Bitcoin. Rollups on Ethereum have flourished in the last five years with L2 transactions far exceeding L1 transactions. Rollups 1. Today high transaction costs on Ethereum seem to be due to conges- tion (low throughput relative to demand) rather than the dollar operational costs of Ethereum nodes collectively. This may also be attributed to Ethereum rewards (inflation) subsidizing operational costs. 1983 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00248 on Bitcoin have only started to take off more recently, partly due to the higher complexity of handling settlement (e.g. verifying proof(s) on Bitcoin). Currently, posting transaction data to Ethereum is the primary cost for operating rollups on Ethereum. Since the L1 nodes do not need to execute rollup transactions, embedding this data as a transaction is actually wasteful, since it is not necessary for every node to see and execute the transactions. Rather, the L1 nodes only need to collectively ensure data availability : that at any point in time, any client can request the system to reconstruct the correct state. In a system like Ethereum, erasure codes make it easy to achieve data availability with significantly less communication than broadcasting the data to all nodes, assuming a maximum threshold of corrupt nodes [12]. Specifically, with N nodes where at most an f fraction are corrupt, and an optimal era- sure code with rate 1−f, it suffices for each node to receive a 1/N slice of the encoded data since there exist at least N(1−f) non-corrupted nodes that are able to reconstruct the original data. The total required communication in this case for a single β-bit blob of data is only O(β/(1 − f)) rather than O(β · N). Ethereum is undergoing changes to its core protocol to support this solution [3]; also, other alternative data availability systems such as EigenDA [4] and Celestia [2] are already in use by rollups. In so-called proof-of-stake systems like Ethereum, data availability with per-participant communication sublinear in the size of the data can be achieved under the same security assumptions as the underlying consensus protocol because both rely on non-corrupt nodes are identifiable by public keys and stay online for a sufficiently long time. However, Bitcoin's consensus protocol, which leverages proof-of-work, has a unique set of characteristics that make it quite different from Ethereum's. Bitcoin is (1) dynamically available under the dynamic participation of nodes; and (2) secure without requiring nodes to authenticate themselves to participate (i.e., is permissionless, which is impossible in pure proof-of-stake-based systems as shown in [33, Theorem 1]). This is in contrast to Ethereum, where participating nodes need to preregister their keys. 2 For Bitcoin rollups to enjoy similar cost savings as Ethereum rollups (reduce both redundant computation and communication) without compromising on these key characteristics, they require a protocol for data availability that achieves sublinear com- munication under these same set of assumptions. Prior to our present work, no data availability system with sublinear communication has been shown to achieve this. Our contribution. In this paper, we close the gap by introducing the first data availability protocol that tolerates dynamic participation and requires no authentication. The only additional assumption we need is the existence of reliable participants (i.e., there are nodes back online even if going offline, within a unknown period of time). This 2. In Ethereum, a node joins the system by purchasing ETH and then “staking” at least 32 ETH [23], which technically requires the cooperation of the counterparty selling ETH and the consensus itself to approve the participant as the staking set member. Circles are messages in our protocol, which are submitted to the SMR protocol as transactions. The black circle is the commitment of a data blob. The green circles are “yes” votes. The purple circles are “no” votes. additional condition is both necessary and sufficient (to reduce communication costs), as discussed in Section 4.2. The resulting scheme is both asymptotically and con- cretely much more efficient than posting the blob directly to layer-1, as evidenced by our analysis and implementation. Specifically, with Bitcoin, the asymptotic communication cost (per participant) grows sublinear in the data blob size. Concretely, the communication cost is reduced by more than 1000x and the latency is also reduced by more than 10x for reasonable parameter chocies. We provide a detailed evaluation in Section 6. Technical overview. We now give an overview of our construction, also illustrated in Figure 1. To propose a data blob (rollup block), the proposer posts a commitment to the data blob to the SMR protocol. Once this commitment is included in the SMR protocol, other participants querying the proposer for data samples of it. Upon getting a response, a participant verifies if the reply is consistent with its request and the commitment posted to the SMR protocol. If so, it posts a “yes” vote to the SMR protocol, represented as a green circle in Figure 1. Otherwise, it submits a “no” vote, represented as a purple circle in Figure 1. In order to vote, participants must also include a small proof of work in their votes3. This is an anti-Sybil mechanism that ensures that malicious participants cannot produce too many fake votes. Participants repeat sampling and voting, until they see the following two conditions are met: (1) at least k new blocks are proposed after the commitment block, and (2) there are more than u votes cast on the commitment. When both are satisfied, participants decide whether a block is available by examining if the difference between the number of “yes” and “no” votes is larger than a given threshold Th. We show that even given an unknown number of partici- pants and no global clock, with carefully analyzed Th, k, u, the following properties hold: (i) an honestly proposed blob is always confirmed as available; (ii) every honest party will always agree on whether or not a blob is available; (iii) every honest party will eventually be able to reconstruct the pro- posed blob if they decide it is available; (iv) communication per participant is sublinear in the blob size.
